questions.scenario: Your friend sprains their ankle during a school football match. What is your first instinct?

options.text: Quickly grab some ice, tape it up, and figure out how fast they can get back in the game.
Check their bone alignment and gently test their joint to see exactly what is strained.
Find them a comfortable way to walk to class without putting weight on it, maybe leaning on a specific bag.
Ask them if they feel any numbness or tingling in their toes to check for nerve damage.

questions.scenario: A favorite gadget or chair in your house is broken. How do you deal with it?

options.text: Upgrade it with stronger parts so it can handle heavy, intense use without breaking again.
Fix the core structural frame so it can properly bear weight and balance again.
Modify it by adding soft grips or changing its shape so it's even easier to use than before.
Carefully untangle the complicated internal wires to restore the main control connection.

questions.scenario: Your grandparents are starting to struggle with walking up the stairs. What is your solution?

options.text: Act like their coach and motivate them to do daily leg exercises to build stamina.
Focus on their knee joints and suggest specific stretches to reduce their stiffness and pain.
Install a sturdy handrail and place non-slip mats so the stairs are safer and easier for them.
Work with them on their balance and brain-body coordination so they don't feel dizzy.

questions.scenario: When you are packing a heavy backpack for a school trip, what is your main focus?

options.text: Packing only the lightweight, high-performance essentials so I can move fast.
Adjusting the straps perfectly so the weight is balanced and doesn't hurt my spine.
Using special pouches and easy-pull zippers so I can grab what I need without struggling.
Mentally mapping exactly where everything is placed so my brain knows the exact layout.

questions.scenario: Which of these video game styles do you enjoy the most?

options.text: Fast-paced sports or action games where speed, reflexes, and performance matter.
Building games where you manage physical structures, mechanics, and physics.
Simulation games where you customize environments and tools to help characters live better.
Complex puzzle games where you have to patiently rewire circuits and unlock pathways.

questions.scenario: You are teaching a younger sibling how to ride a bicycle. What is your teaching style?

options.text: Cheering them on loudly, running beside them, and pushing them to go faster.
Checking the seat height and handlebar alignment to make sure their posture is correct.
Adding training wheels and knee pads to adapt the bike until they feel confident.
Patiently explaining how to balance and letting their brain slowly learn the muscle memory.

questions.scenario: You have a massive, complicated project to finish for school. How do you handle it?

options.text: Push through it in a high-energy, intense burst of pure focus.
Break it down into solid structural parts and build the foundation first.
Find a creative tool or a unique 'hack' to make the workload much easier.
Patiently untangle the complex instructions step-by-step, no matter how long it takes.

questions.scenario: What kind of YouTube video are you most likely to watch when you are bored?

options.text: Athletes recovering from crazy injuries and returning to win championships.
Chiropractors cracking backs or detailed explanations of how human joints work.
Cool life hacks, DIY tools, and gadgets that make everyday chores effortless.
Medical miracles of people slowly re-learning to walk or speak after brain injuries.

questions.scenario: If you were to invent a new piece of wearable technology, what would it do?

options.text: A sleeve that instantly boosts muscle recovery and tracking for athletes.
A smart-brace that perfectly aligns your spine and joints to eliminate all body pain.
A robotic glove that helps people with weak hands easily grip everyday objects like pens and spoons.
A headband that stimulates the brain's nerves to help heal paralysis or improve balance.

questions.scenario: Which of these moments would make you feel the most proud?

options.text: Helping a superstar player get back on the field just in time for the finals.
Seeing someone who was bent over in pain finally stand up completely straight and smile.
Watching a child with disabilities feed themselves independently for the first time.
Seeing a patient who was paralyzed finally twitch their finger after months of hard work.

Sports_Physiotherapist.title: Sports Physiotherapist
Sports_Physiotherapist.primary_match_text: You are highly energetic, fast-paced, and goal-oriented. You thrive in high-pressure environments and love pushing physical limits.
Sports_Physiotherapist.day_in_the_life: Standing on the sidelines of a major sporting event, rushing onto the field to treat injured athletes, and designing intense gym routines to get players back to peak performance.
Sports_Physiotherapist.alternative_match_text: With your focus on high performance and physical mechanics, a career in Strength and Conditioning Coaching or Sports Science is a perfect alternative.
Sports_Physiotherapist.roadmap: Take Science (PCB) in 11th/12th. Pursue a Bachelor of Physiotherapy (BPT - 4.5 years), followed by a Master of Physiotherapy (MPT) specializing in Sports.

Orthopedic_Physiotherapist.title: Orthopedic Physiotherapist
Orthopedic_Physiotherapist.primary_match_text: You have a highly structural mind. You think like a human mechanic, focusing on how bones, joints, and muscles align and bear weight.
Orthopedic_Physiotherapist.day_in_the_life: Working in a clinic, helping a teenager recover from knee surgery, or correcting the spine posture of someone with severe back pain using manual therapy and specific exercises.
Orthopedic_Physiotherapist.alternative_match_text: Because you are fascinated by human structure and mechanics, Biomechanics, Ergonomics, or even Prosthetics (designing artificial limbs) are great parallel paths.
Orthopedic_Physiotherapist.roadmap: Take Science (PCB) in 11th/12th. Pursue a Bachelor of Physiotherapy (BPT - 4.5 years), followed by a Master of Physiotherapy (MPT) specializing in Orthopedics.

Occupational_Therapist.title: Occupational Therapist
Occupational_Therapist.primary_match_text: You are a creative problem solver with a ton of empathy. Instead of just fixing the body, you love adapting the environment and tools to make life easier.
Occupational_Therapist.day_in_the_life: Designing special grips for a stroke patient so they can hold a spoon, teaching children with autism how to process sensory information, or recommending home modifications for the elderly.
Occupational_Therapist.alternative_match_text: Since you love designing practical solutions for daily challenges, fields like Rehabilitation Engineering or Special Education are highly rewarding alternatives.
Occupational_Therapist.roadmap: Take Science (PCB) in 11th/12th. Pursue a Bachelor of Occupational Therapy (BOT - 4.5 years), followed by a Master's (MOT) if you wish to specialize in pediatrics or neuro.

Neurological_Physiotherapist.title: Neurological Physiotherapist
Neurological_Physiotherapist.primary_match_text: You are incredibly patient and fascinated by complex systems. You understand that healing the brain and nerves takes time, focus, and deep rewiring.
Neurological_Physiotherapist.day_in_the_life: Working closely with stroke survivors or patients with spinal cord injuries, slowly retraining their brains to balance, walk, and reconnect with their paralyzed limbs.
Neurological_Physiotherapist.alternative_match_text: With your patience and interest in the brain-body connection, studying Neuroscience, Cognitive Rehabilitation, or Clinical Neurophysiology are excellent backup paths.
Neurological_Physiotherapist.roadmap: Take Science (PCB) in 11th/12th. Pursue a Bachelor of Physiotherapy (BPT - 4.5 years), followed by a Master of Physiotherapy (MPT) specializing in Neurology.
